Delta-rho-omicron; the root ἀνδρ- means 'man, husband, warrior'.
Long epsilon (eta) with acute [méː] — the pitch peak and a ruler's domain.
Delta-eta, long final syllable; the name ends in the feminine agent suffix.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ahn-dro-MAY-day' — the third syllable is pitched and drawn out; the final -ē is long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἀνδρομέδη (Andromédē), from ἀνδρ- 'man' + μέδω 'rule, provide for' — 'she who rules men'

kin.label: Ancient alternative
kin.form: Some ancient readers heard 'she who is mindful of men' — the scholia already debate the compound

kin.label: Persian genealogy
kin.form: Herodotus 7.61, 7.150 — her son Persēs is made the eponymous ancestor of the Persian kings

pronunciation.note: Andromédē is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀνδρομέδη contains both stress (acute on the long η) and length (η). The compound is transparently Greek, though the princess herself is said to dwell in Ethiopia.

domains.title: The Chained Princess
domains.subtitle: Rescue, Constellation, Royal Sacrifice
domains.lead: Andromédē is the princess chained to a sea-rock, offered to a monster and saved by a hero. Her myth is one of the most widely reproduced rescue narratives in Western art, and her catasterism placed her among the stars forever.

cards.name: Royal Daughter
cards.desc: Daughter of Kepheus and Kassiepeia, rulers of Aithiopia; her lineage is royal and unfortunate.

cards.name: Sacrifice to the Sea
cards.desc: Chained to a coastal rock as appeasement to the ketos sent by Poseidôn.

cards.name: Perseus's Rescue
cards.desc: Saved by the gorgon-slayer, she becomes his wife and, through their son Persēs, ancestor of the Persian line (Herodotus 7.61).

cards.name: Constellation
cards.desc: Placed in the northern sky after death, she keeps the whole family group as stars; the Andromeda galaxy is her stellar home.

symbols.name: Sea-rock and chains
symbols.meaning: Her exposure to the ketos and the vulnerability of innocence before power

symbols.name: Mirror of Kassiepeia
symbols.meaning: The boast that set the myth in motion: her mother's claim to surpass the Nereids

symbols.name: Head of Medousa
symbols.meaning: The weapon Perseus carries when he rescues her — and turns back her own kinsmen

symbols.name: Wedding crown
symbols.meaning: Her marriage to Perseus and catasterism into the northern sky

mythology.lead: Andromédē's story is a chain of consequences: a queen's boast, a god's wrath, a daughter's punishment, and a hero's arrival at the decisive moment. It is also a founding myth of genealogy, linking Greek and Persian royal lines.

myths.title: The Queen Who Rivaled the Nereids
myths.text: The chain begins with a boast. Kassiepeia, queen of Aithiopia, declared that she — or, in some tellings, her daughter — was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea-nymphs in Poseidôn's train (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.3; the fullest telling is Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.663–764). The insulted sea answered with a flood and a ketos, a ravening sea-beast against the Ethiopian coast, and the oracle of Zeus-Ammōn delivered the verdict: only the exposure of Andromédē, the king's daughter, would end the devastation. Kepheus, pressed by his starving people, had the princess stripped and chained to a sea-cliff as the monster's due. Sophocles wrote an Andromeda, now lost but for fragments, and painted vases carried the scene to every Greek city. The myth's logic is pitiless: the daughter pays for the mother's tongue, and the sea, which the Greeks both crossed and feared, collects its tribute in royal flesh.

myths.title: The Maiden and the Winged Stranger
myths.text: Andromédē was fastened to the rock by bonds Ovid calls indissoluble — the Nereids' own handiwork, in his exquisite cruelty — and left to the rising beast. At that moment Perseus came flying home from the Gorgons' shore, with Hermes' harpe, Athena's mirrored shield, and the kibisis on his shoulders. Struck by the chained figure — a statue, 'but for the wind in her hair and the tears on her cheeks' (Ovid, Met. 4.672–679) — he struck a bargain with Kepheus: the girl's life for her hand. The scene proved irresistible to Greek painters: from early Corinthian and Attic vases to the frescoes of Pompeii, the pale maiden against dark rock, the descending hero, and the monster breasting the foam became antiquity's canonical rescue image. Innocence displayed and violence arriving in the same instant — the myth compresses the whole psychology of the heroic moment into one shoreline.

myths.title: Phineus and the Fight for the Bride
myths.text: The rescue did not end the story. Andromédē had been promised to her uncle Phineus, and while the wedding feast of Perseus and Andromédē was still singing, Phineus burst in with an armed mob to claim her. Outnumbered, Perseus unslung the kibisis and turned the Gorgoneion on the attackers, transforming Phineus and his men into a stone tableau mid-swing — Ovid lingers over the frozen weapons and marble mouths (Metamorphoses 5.1–249; Apollodorus 2.4.3 gives the sober prose version). The slaughter shadowed the marriage it defended: Andromédē's deliverance was purchased in her kinsmen's blood, a price the myth does not hide. She bore Perseus many sons, among them Persēs, whom Herodotus (7.61) makes the eponymous ancestor of the Persian kings — folding a Greek princess into the genealogy of an empire. The rescued become the founders; the monster's intended bride mothers a royal line.

myths.title: Catasterism and the Great Galaxy
myths.text: At death, Athena set Andromédē among the stars — the 'chained lady' of the northern sky, as Eratosthenes' Catasterismi and Hyginus' De Astronomica (2.11) preserve the tale. The constellation keeps the whole family on stage: Perseus above her with the Gorgon's head, Kepheus and Kassiepeia on either hand, and the ketos — our Cetus — still rising from the sea below, the pursuit made permanent. The Great Andromeda Galaxy, M31, the nearest spiral galaxy to our own, bears her name, so that the princess exposed to a sea-monster now names an island universe two and a half million light-years away. Catasterism is the Greeks' quiet answer to mortality: what could not be saved on earth is preserved in the pattern of the sky, where the chains are drawn as stars and no god's wrath can reach her again.

lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted Andromeda without renaming her; she is one of the few Greek mythic figures to enter Latin poetry under her original form. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance she became an emblem of rescue, feminine beauty in distress, and the redemptive hero. Modern astronomy keeps her constellation and galaxy names intact. Some scholars compare her Near Eastern analogues — the exposed princess, the sea-monster combat — but the Greek narrative is distinctively tied to Perseus and the Argolid-Persian genealogy.
lore.culturalLegacy: Andromeda is the archetype of the damsel in distress and the catasterized heroine. From Titian and Rubens to Victorian painting and modern fantasy, her image persists: the chained woman, the arriving savior, the monster from the deep. The Andromeda Galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, carries her name into astrophysics, making her one of the few Greek figures whose cultural reach extends beyond the solar system.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Andromeda is not a willing victim; she is the price of someone else's pride. Her passivity on the rock is not weakness but the consequence of a cosmic transaction in which she had no voice. The myth therefore asks us to look at the people sacrificed to appease forces they did not create.

Yet her rescue is also the myth's redemption. Perseus does not merely slay the monster; he sees her, chooses her, and makes her his equal in marriage. In that moment, the object of sacrifice becomes a queen and a star. Andromeda reminds us that dignity can survive exposure, and that the gaze that recognizes suffering can also transform it.
lore.archaeology: The myth of Andromeda was popular in Greek and Roman visual culture. Painted vases show Perseus approaching the chained maiden; Roman wall paintings and sarcophagi reproduce the rescue scene. The constellation was mapped by Ptolemy and transmitted through Arabic and Renaissance star catalogs. No single archaeological site claims to be her rock, though Joppa (modern Jaffa) was identified with the location in antiquity.
